title: Upper GI bleeding
blurb: Recognise and resuscitate an upper GI bleed, use the Blatchford and Rockall scores, and apply NICE CG141 on transfusion, endoscopy timing, PPIs and variceal bleeding.
question: Mr O'Brien, 56, has known liver cirrhosis and vomits fresh blood in the emergency department. His pulse is 118 and BP 92/58. Besides resuscitation, which two treatments does NICE recommend at presentation for a suspected variceal bleed?

teach.body: An upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleed comes from the oesophagus, stomach or duodenum. It shows as haematemesis (vomiting fresh blood or 'coffee grounds') and melaena (black, tarry, offensive stool). Common causes are peptic ulcers, often linked to NSAIDs, and oesophageal varices in liver disease. Plain English: a fast pulse and falling blood pressure in someone vomiting blood is shock until proven otherwise, and the first job is resuscitation.

steps.label: Resuscitate
steps.sub: ABCDE, NEWS2, IV access, bloods, fluids

steps.label: Endoscopy
steps.sub: Immediately after resuscitation if unstable; 24 h for others

steps.label: After
steps.sub: Full Rockall; PPI if stigmata seen

head: Give
When
rows: Massive bleeding: local major haemorrhage protocol
Actively bleeding and platelets below 50 x 10⁹/L
Actively bleeding, PT/INR or APTT above 1.5 x normal
teach.caption: No platelets if not actively bleeding and haemodynamically stable. Over-transfusion may be as damaging as under-transfusion.

teach.body: Offer endoscopy immediately after resuscitation to unstable patients with severe bleeding, and within 24 hours of admission to everyone else. Do not give proton pump inhibitors (or H2-receptor antagonists) before endoscopy for suspected non-variceal bleeding. After endoscopy, offer a PPI to people with non-variceal bleeding and stigmata of recent haemorrhage.

teach.text: The instinct to 'start a PPI drip' straight away is wrong under CG141: no acid suppression before endoscopy in suspected non-variceal bleeding. The things that ARE started at presentation are for suspected VARICEAL bleeding: terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics.

children.label: Terlipressin + prophylactic antibiotics
children.sub: At presentation; band ligation for oesophageal varices

children.label: No PPI before endoscopy
children.sub: PPI after if stigmata of recent haemorrhage

teach.caption: Terlipressin is stopped after definitive haemostasis or after 5 days (CG141 1.5.1).

teach.h: Medicines review in upper GI bleeding (CG141 1.6)
items: Continue low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention once haemostasis is achieved.
Stop other NSAIDs, including COX-2 inhibitors, during the acute phase.
Discuss continuing clopidogrel with the relevant specialist (e.g. cardiology or stroke) and the patient.
On warfarin and actively bleeding: prothrombin complex concentrate; follow local warfarin protocol once bleeding stops.

teach.h: Scenario: Mrs Lewis on the medical assessment unit
teach.body: Mrs Lewis, 74, takes naproxen for arthritis and aspirin after a stent. She has melaena and feels faint: pulse 112, BP 98/60, NEWS2 rising. The nurse escalates, assists with ABCDE and two large-bore cannulae, sends bloods including crossmatch, and starts prescribed fluids. She does not give a PPI before endoscopy. Naproxen is stopped; after endoscopy controls the ulcer bleed, low-dose aspirin is continued and a PPI started.

items: Blatchford at first assessment; full Rockall after endoscopy; Blatchford 0 can mean early discharge.
Platelets if bleeding and below 50; FFP if PT/APTT above 1.5 x normal; cryo if fibrinogen below 1.5.
Endoscopy immediately after resuscitation if unstable; within 24 hours for others.
No PPI before endoscopy in non-variceal bleeding; PPI after if stigmata.
Suspected varices: terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics at presentation.

summary: You can now recognise and help resuscitate a person with an upper GI bleed, apply the Blatchford and Rockall scores at the right time, and follow CG141 on blood products and endoscopy timing. You can also avoid pre-endoscopy PPIs and start variceal treatment promptly.

A.q: Mr O'Brien, 56, has cirrhosis and haematemesis. His pulse is 118 and BP 92/58. Which treatments does NICE recommend at presentation for suspected variceal bleeding?
options: IV proton pump inhibitor and tranexamic acid
A.why: NICE CG141 recs 1.5.1–1.5.2: offer terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotic therapy at presentation to people with suspected variceal bleeding.

whyNot.1: PPIs are not the presentation treatment for varices, and tranexamic acid is not a CG141 recommendation.
whyNot.2: Platelets are given when actively bleeding with a count below 50; the count is not given here.
whyNot.3: These are not the acute presentation treatments in CG141.

A.q: When should the Glasgow-Blatchford score be used for a person with acute upper GI bleeding?
A.why: NICE CG141 rec 1.1.1: use the Blatchford score at first assessment and the full Rockall score after endoscopy.

whyNot.0: The full Rockall score is the one used after endoscopy.
whyNot.1: Risk scoring guides early management, not discharge paperwork.
whyNot.3: The score is calculated at first assessment, not after transfusion.

A.q: Mrs Lewis has suspected non-variceal upper GI bleeding and is awaiting endoscopy. The junior doctor asks whether to start an IV proton pump inhibitor now. What does CG141 say?
options: Start a PPI infusion straight away
Give an oral PPI with food
Do not give acid suppression before endoscopy
A.why: NICE CG141 rec 1.4.3: do not offer acid-suppression drugs (PPIs or H2-receptor antagonists) before endoscopy to people with suspected non-variceal upper GI bleeding.

whyNot.0: Pre-endoscopy PPI is specifically not recommended.
whyNot.1: H2-receptor antagonists are also named as not to be given before endoscopy.
whyNot.2: Any acid-suppression drug before endoscopy is not recommended; she should also be nil by mouth for endoscopy.

B.q: A haemodynamically stable man with upper GI bleeding is not actively bleeding. His platelets are 42 x 10⁹/L. What does CG141 advise about platelet transfusion?
options: Give platelets to keep them above 50
Give one pool and recheck in 1 hour
B.why: NICE CG141 rec 1.2.3: do not offer platelet transfusion to patients who are not actively bleeding and are haemodynamically stable.

whyNot.0: The below-50 threshold applies to people who are actively bleeding.
whyNot.1: Endoscopy alone is not an indication when he is stable and not bleeding.
whyNot.3: Transfusion is not indicated in this situation.

B.q: Mrs Tan is actively bleeding from an upper GI source. Her INR is 2.1 (not on anticoagulants) and fibrinogen is 1.2 g/L after FFP. Which product should be offered next?
B.why: NICE CG141 rec 1.2.4: offer FFP if actively bleeding with PT/INR or APTT above 1.5 x normal; if fibrinogen remains below 1.5 g/L despite FFP, offer cryoprecipitate as well.

whyNot.1: Platelets are for a count below 50 in active bleeding; no count is given here.
whyNot.2: Vitamin K is not the CG141 product for a low fibrinogen.

B.q: Mr Grant was admitted with a stable upper GI bleed at 20:00 on Monday. By when should he have an endoscopy?
B.why: NICE CG141 rec 1.3.2: offer endoscopy within 24 hours of admission to all patients other than those who are unstable with severe bleeding.

whyNot.0: Immediate endoscopy (after resuscitation) is for unstable patients with severe bleeding.
whyNot.3: A routine list may be days away; the limit is 24 hours.

C.q: Mrs Lewis, 74, takes naproxen and low-dose aspirin after a coronary stent. Endoscopy has stopped her ulcer bleeding. What should happen to these medicines?
C.why: NICE CG141 recs 1.6.1–1.6.2: continue low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention once haemostasis is achieved, and stop other NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors) during the acute phase.

whyNot.0: Stopping aspirin after a stent raises thrombotic risk; CG141 continues it.
whyNot.1: Naproxen is an NSAID and must be stopped in the acute phase.
whyNot.3: This reverses the guidance: naproxen stops, aspirin continues.

C.q: Mr Hassan, 48, has had a single small coffee-ground vomit. He is well, with normal observations and bloods, and his pre-endoscopy Blatchford score is 0. What does NICE suggest?
C.why: NICE CG141 rec 1.1.2: consider early discharge for patients with a pre-endoscopy Blatchford score of 0.

whyNot.0: Immediate endoscopy is for unstable patients with severe bleeding.
whyNot.1: A score of 0 identifies low risk, supporting early discharge rather than admission.
whyNot.2: Transfusion is guided by the clinical picture, and he is well with normal bloods.

C.q: Mr O'Brien has suspected variceal bleeding and remains hypotensive after initial fluids. The registrar plans endoscopy. Which timing is correct?
C.why: NICE CG141 rec 1.3.1: offer endoscopy to unstable patients with severe acute upper GI bleeding immediately after resuscitation.

whyNot.0: 24 hours is for patients who are not unstable with severe bleeding.
whyNot.2: Waiting for a normal INR delays urgent endoscopy; clotting is corrected alongside.
whyNot.3: 5 days is the maximum terlipressin course, not the endoscopy time.

reteach.title: Two roads from the same vomit
reteach.question: Picture the person vomiting blood standing at a fork. One road is variceal, the other non-variceal. What is done on each road before the camera?

blocks.body: Both roads start with resuscitation and a Blatchford score. On the variceal road (liver disease), start terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics at presentation. On the non-variceal road (often an NSAID ulcer), hold acid suppression until after endoscopy, then give a PPI if stigmata are seen. Both roads reach endoscopy: immediately after resuscitation if unstable, otherwise within 24 hours.

blocks.text: Blatchford before the scope, Rockall after it.

explain.body: Glasgow-Blatchford at first assessment; full Rockall after endoscopy. Consider early discharge with a pre-endoscopy Blatchford of 0.

test.q: Which score is calculated in full after endoscopy for upper GI bleeding?
test.why: NICE CG141 rec 1.1.1: the full Rockall score is used after endoscopy.

whyNot.0: NEWS2 tracks deterioration but is not the CG141 risk score.
whyNot.2: Wells scores estimate DVT and PE probability.
whyNot.3: CHA2DS2-VASc estimates stroke risk in AF.

explain.body: Massive bleeding: local protocol. Platelets if actively bleeding and below 50. FFP if PT/INR or APTT above 1.5 x normal. Cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen stays below 1.5 g/L. PCC if on warfarin and actively bleeding.

test.q: A man on warfarin has active upper GI bleeding. Which product does CG141 recommend?
test.why: NICE CG141 rec 1.2.5: offer prothrombin complex concentrate to patients taking warfarin who are actively bleeding.

whyNot.0: Warfarin affects clotting factors, not platelets.
whyNot.2: Cryoprecipitate is for low fibrinogen despite FFP.

explain.body: Unstable with severe bleeding: endoscopy immediately after resuscitation. Others: within 24 hours of admission. No PPI or H2RA before endoscopy in suspected non-variceal bleeding; PPI after if stigmata of recent haemorrhage.

test.q: After endoscopy shows a non-variceal ulcer with stigmata of recent haemorrhage, what does CG141 recommend?
test.why: NICE CG141 rec 1.4.4: offer PPIs to people with non-variceal bleeding and stigmata of recent haemorrhage shown at endoscopy.

whyNot.2: Acid suppression is withheld before endoscopy, not after stigmata are seen.
whyNot.3: NSAIDs are stopped in the acute phase.

explain.body: Terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics at presentation. Band ligation for oesophageal varices. Stop terlipressin after definitive haemostasis or after 5 days.

test.q: Which endoscopic treatment does NICE recommend for bleeding oesophageal varices?
test.why: NICE CG141 rec 1.5.3: use band ligation for upper GI bleeding from oesophageal varices.

whyNot.0: Clips are a CG141 option for non-variceal bleeding, not varices.
whyNot.1: Thermal coagulation with adrenaline is a non-variceal option.
whyNot.2: Fibrin or thrombin with adrenaline is a non-variceal option.
